examples.en: The villain in the movie brainwashes people.
That group brainwashed young students.
Methods of brainwashing people are dangerous.

examples.ko: 광고가 우리를 세뇌한다고 느낄 때가 있어요.
examples.en: Sometimes I feel that ads are brainwashing us.
No one can brainwash me.
They brainwashed an elderly person and took the property.

explain: 세뇌하다는 생각을 억지로 바꾸는 나쁜 일에만 써요. 좋은 내용을 알려 줄 때는 '교육하다'나 '가르치다'를 써요. 당하는 쪽은 '세뇌당하다'라고 해요.
explain_en: 세뇌하다 is only for forcing ideas on someone in a bad way. When passing on good content, use 교육하다 or 가르치다. The person on the receiving end is described with 세뇌당하다.

examples.en: Protein is made up of many amino acids.
This drink contains amino acids.

examples.ko: 운동한 뒤에 아미노산을 먹는 사람이 많아요.
examples.en: Many people take amino acids after exercising.
You get the amino acids your body needs from food.
Shall I buy an amino acid supplement?
We learned about the structure of amino acids in science class.

explain: 아미노산은 과학, 건강, 운동 이야기에서 나와요. 일상 대화에서는 '단백질'이 훨씬 자주 나오고, 아미노산은 보충제나 식품 포장에서 많이 봐요. '필수 아미노산'처럼 앞에 말이 붙는 경우가 많아요.
explain_en: 아미노산 appears in science, health, and fitness talk. In everyday conversation 단백질 (protein) comes up far more often, while 아미노산 shows up on supplements and food packaging. It often comes with a word in front, as in 필수 아미노산 (essential amino acid).

examples.en: A seizure notice was stuck on the house.
I was shocked to hear about the bank account seizure.
The court decided on the seizure.

examples.ko: 압류가 풀리면 돈을 쓸 수 있어요.
examples.en: Once the seizure is lifted, you can use the money.

examples.ko: 세금을 안 내서 차에 압류가 걸렸어요.
examples.en: Because the tax wasn't paid, the car was placed under seizure.
A seizure notice came by mail.

explain: 압류는 재산을 묶어 두기만 해요. 실제로 팔아서 빚을 갚는 단계는 '경매'라고 해요. 뉴스에서는 '가압류'도 같이 나오는데, 임시로 먼저 묶어 두는 걸 가리켜요.
explain_en: 압류 only freezes the property so it cannot be sold or moved. The later step of actually selling it to pay the debt is called 경매. In the news you also see 가압류, which is a provisional freeze made in advance.

examples.en: The court seized that person's house.
The tax office seizes the bank account.

examples.ko: 빚을 못 갚으면 월급도 압류할 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you can't repay the debt, they can even seize your salary.

examples.ko: 은행이 차를 압류해서 운전을 못 해요.
examples.en: The bank seized the car, so I can't drive.

examples.ko: 재산을 압류하는 일은 아무나 할 수 없어요.
examples.en: Not just anyone can seize property.

examples.ko: 세금을 안 내면 재산을 압류한다고 했어요.
examples.en: They said they would seize your property if you don't pay taxes.

explain: 압류하다는 법원, 세무서, 은행 같은 기관이 하는 일이라 개인이 주어면 어색해요. 개인이 남의 물건을 가져가는 건 '뺏다'나 '가져가다'라고 해요. 당하는 쪽은 '압류당하다'라고 말해요.
explain_en: 압류하다 is done by institutions such as a court, tax office, or bank, so it sounds odd with a private person as the subject. When an individual takes someone's things, 뺏다 or 가져가다 is used. The person it happens to is described with 압류당하다.

examples.ko: 길에서 떠는 고양이를 보고 연민을 느꼈어요.
examples.en: I felt compassion when I saw a cat shivering on the street.
I looked at the child with pity.
I felt sorry for my friend's situation, and compassion welled up.
It wasn't out of pity that I helped.

examples.ko: 그 영화는 악당에게도 연민을 느끼게 해요.
examples.en: The movie makes you feel pity even for the villain.
I was comforted in a voice full of compassion.

explain: 연민은 상대의 아픔을 같이 느끼는 따뜻한 마음에 가까워요. 비슷한 '동정'은 내려다보는 느낌이 들 수 있어서 상대가 싫어할 때도 있어요. 보통 '연민을 느끼다', '연민을 갖다'처럼 써요.
explain_en: 연민 is close to a warm feeling of sharing someone's pain. The similar word 동정 can feel like looking down on the person, so people sometimes dislike receiving it. It is usually used as 연민을 느끼다 or 연민을 갖다.

examples.en: This city has many canals.
Boats move slowly along the canal.

examples.ko: 파나마 운하는 두 바다를 이어 줘요.
examples.en: The Panama Canal connects two oceans.
I walked along the path beside the canal.
People in the past carried goods by canal.
The water in the canal has become clean.

explain: 자연에 있는 물길은 '강'이나 '개천'이라고 하고, 배가 다니거나 물을 보내려고 사람이 판 물길만 운하라고 해요. '파나마 운하', '수에즈 운하'처럼 이름 뒤에 붙여요.
explain_en: A waterway that occurs in nature is called 강 or 개천. Only a channel dug by people for ships or for moving water is called 운하. It follows the name, as in 파나마 운하 and 수에즈 운하.

examples.ko: 가을이 되면 벼 이삭이 노랗게 익어요.
examples.en: In autumn the rice ears ripen to yellow.

examples.ko: 농부가 밀 이삭을 한 줌 잘라 왔어요.
examples.en: The farmer cut a handful of wheat ears and brought them.
The ears of grain bow their heads as they ripen.
I carefully picked up even the ears that had fallen in the field.
The wind blows between the barley ears.
I shook the grains of rice off the ear.

explain: 이삭은 벼, 보리, 밀처럼 곡식 줄기 끝에만 써요. 과일이나 채소에 달린 건 '열매'라고 해요. '벼 이삭', '보리 이삭'처럼 곡식 이름을 앞에 붙여요. 성경 속 인물 이름(Isaac)도 같은 글자예요.
explain_en: 이삭 is used only for the top of a grain stalk such as rice, barley, or wheat. What hangs on fruit or vegetable plants is called 열매. The grain name goes in front, as in 벼 이삭 and 보리 이삭. The Bible name Isaac is written with the same letters.

examples.en: Let's hear the opinions of teachers working on the front line.
The chairman stepped back from active duty last year.

examples.ko: 일선의 직원들이 가장 먼저 문제를 알아요.
examples.en: The staff on the front line are the first to know about problems.

examples.ko: 대표님이 일선으로 돌아와서 직접 현장을 봤어요.
examples.en: The CEO came back to the front line and saw the site in person.
Nurses work day and night on the hospital front line.
People on the front line are always busy.

explain: 일선은 본부나 윗선과 달리 학교·병원·경찰서 같은 현장에서 직접 일하는 자리예요. '일선 교사', '일선 경찰'처럼 사람 앞에 붙여 써요. '현장'보다 조직 안의 위아래 관계가 더 느껴지고, '최일선'은 그중에서도 가장 앞에 있는 곳을 가리켜요. '일선에서 물러나다'는 은퇴하거나 직접 실무를 맡지 않게 될 때 써요.
explain_en: Unlike the head office or upper management, 일선 is the position where people work directly on site, such as in schools, hospitals, or police stations. It is attached before a person, as in 일선 교사 and 일선 경찰. Compared with 현장, it carries more of a sense of hierarchy within an organization, and 최일선 points to the very frontmost part of it. 일선에서 물러나다 is used when someone retires or no longer handles hands-on work directly.

examples.en: This transaction is completely legal.
They made the arrest through lawful procedures.
I asked a lawyer whether that method is legal.

examples.ko: 허가 없이 찍은 사진은 적법하지 않아요.
examples.en: Photos taken without permission are not lawful.
If it had been legal, it wouldn't have been a problem.
The money was earned legally, so I'm not worried.

explain: 적법하다는 뉴스, 재판, 계약서처럼 딱딱한 자리에서 주로 써요. 일상에서는 '합법이에요'가 더 자연스러워요. 반대말은 '위법하다'예요. '적법한 절차', '적법하게'처럼 뒤의 말을 꾸미는 형태로 자주 나와요.
explain_en: 적법하다 is used mostly in formal settings such as news, trials, and contracts. In daily talk, 합법이에요 sounds more natural. The opposite is 위법하다. It often appears in forms that modify what follows, like 적법한 절차 and 적법하게.

en: tribal chief; patriarch (head of a clan)

examples.en: The tribe's chief held a meeting.
The chief gathered the tribe and spoke to them.
I met the chief of an African tribe.
The chief's daughter is the main character of the story.

examples.ko: 젊은 나이에 족장이 된 사람을 알아요.
examples.en: I know someone who became a chief at a young age.
I gave a gift to the chief.

explain: 족장은 한 부족이나 큰 집안의 우두머리예요. 비슷한 '추장'은 원주민 부족 이야기에서 주로 쓰고, 마을을 대표하는 사람은 '촌장'이라고 해요. 한국 시골 마을에서는 '이장'이라고 불러요.
explain_en: 족장 is the head of a tribe or a large clan. The similar 추장 is mostly used in stories about indigenous tribes, and the representative of a village is 촌장. In Korean farming villages, that person is called 이장.

examples.en: The date of release has been set.

examples.ko: 출소 후에 새 일을 찾고 있어요.
examples.en: I'm looking for a new job after being released.
There is an organization that helps people who have been released from prison.
The family is waiting for my uncle's release.
On the day of release, the family came out to meet him.
I worry more about life after release.

explain: 출소는 교도소에서 나오는 일에만 써요. 재판 중에 보증금을 내고 잠시 나오는 건 '보석'이에요. 들어가는 일은 '수감'이라고 해요.
explain_en: 출소 is used only for coming out of prison. Coming out temporarily during a trial by paying a deposit is 보석. Going in is called 수감.

en: be filled with (a feeling); be full of

examples.en: My heart is filled with happiness.
I want to spend a fulfilling day.
I was so full of confidence that I wasn't nervous.
The concert hall was filled with excitement.
I feel a heart full of gratitude.
When I'm full of joy, I start singing.

explain: 충만하다는 행복, 자신감, 기쁨, 사랑처럼 눈에 안 보이는 감정이나 기운에 써요. 컵에 물이 가득한 건 '가득하다'나 '차다'를 써요. 보통 '~으로 충만하다'로 말해요.
explain_en: 충만하다 is for invisible feelings and energy such as happiness, confidence, joy, and love. A cup full of water is 가득하다 or 차다. It usually appears as '~으로 충만하다'.

en: soil and sand; earth and sand (debris)

examples.en: It rained a lot, and soil and sand flowed down.
The road was blocked by earth and sand.
At the construction site, soil and sand are moved by truck.
We cleared the sediment piled up on the riverbed.

examples.ko: 토사 유출을 막기 위해 나무를 심었어요.
examples.en: We planted trees to stop soil from washing away.
I'm worried that soil will pour down the mountain slope.

explain: 토사는 산사태, 홍수, 공사 뉴스에서 자주 들어요. 일상에서는 '흙'과 '모래'를 따로 말하고, 둘이 섞인 덩어리를 한꺼번에 말할 때 토사를 써요. '토사 유출'처럼 붙어 나와요. 의학에서 구토와 설사를 뜻하는 '토사'(吐瀉)는 소리만 같고 한자가 다른 말이에요.
explain_en: 토사 is common in news about landslides, floods, and construction. In daily speech 흙 (soil) and 모래 (sand) are named separately, and 토사 is used for the mixed mass. It appears in phrases like 토사 유출. The medical 토사 (吐瀉), meaning vomiting and diarrhea, sounds the same but is written with different Chinese characters.

examples.en: The sun was strong, so I put on arm sleeves.
You need arm covers when doing farm work.

examples.ko: 자전거용 토시는 팔을 시원하게 해 줘요.
examples.en: Cycling arm sleeves keep your arms cool.
I bought gloves and arm sleeves too.
How much is a pair of arm sleeves?
Sweat built up inside the arm sleeves, so I took them off.

explain: 토시는 손목에서 팔꿈치 사이만 덮어요. 햇빛을 막거나 일할 때 소매를 보호하려고 써요. 장갑과 달리 손가락은 덮지 않아요. 입는 게 아니라 '끼다'나 '하다'라고 말해요.
explain_en: 토시 covers only the forearm, between the wrist and the elbow. It is worn to block the sun or to protect the sleeves while working. Unlike gloves, it does not cover the fingers. It is not 입다 but 끼다 or 하다.

examples.en: The general gave the order to retreat.
Many soldiers were hurt on the road of the retreat.
Everyone was surprised by the news of the sudden retreat.
Deciding on a retreat is not easy.
The retreat was delayed, so the damage grew.
The retreat was carried out in secret.

explain: 퇴각은 군대나 싸움에서 뒤로 물러날 때 써요. 비슷한 '후퇴'는 경기 후퇴처럼 일상이나 경제에도 쓰지만, 퇴각은 주로 전쟁 이야기에서 나와요. 군대를 거두어 빠지는 건 '철수'라고도 해요.
explain_en: 퇴각 is used when an army or a side in a fight pulls back. The similar 후퇴 is also used in daily life and economics, as in 경기 후퇴, but 퇴각 mostly appears in war stories. Pulling troops out can also be called 철수.

examples.en: The enemy army retreated during the night.
The army retreats toward the mountain.
When it started to rain, the unit began to retreat.
The faces of the retreating soldiers were gloomy.
The staff officers said they must retreat quickly.
After the enemy retreated, the village became quiet.

explain: 퇴각하다는 군대 이야기에 주로 써서 일상에서는 '물러나다'를 더 자주 써요. 회의에서 의견을 접거나 약속에서 빠질 때는 '물러나다'나 '빠지다'를 쓰고 퇴각하다는 쓰지 않아요.
explain_en: 퇴각하다 is mainly for military stories, so in daily life 물러나다 is used more often. Giving up an opinion in a meeting or dropping out of a plan is 물러나다 or 빠지다, never 퇴각하다.

examples.en: The bridge could not bear the load.
This shelf's load limit is 20 kilograms.

examples.ko: 하중이 한쪽에 몰리면 무너질 수 있어요.
examples.en: If the load is concentrated on one side, it can collapse.
The floor sank a little because of the load.
The truck unloaded cargo to reduce the load.
When snow piles up, the load on the roof increases.

explain: 하중은 건물, 다리, 선반처럼 구조물이 버티는 무게예요. 사람 몸무게나 물건 무게는 보통 '무게'라고 하고, 하중은 구조가 견디는 힘을 이야기할 때 나와요. '최대 하중'은 안전 표시에서 자주 봐요.
explain_en: 하중 is the weight that a structure such as a building, bridge, or shelf has to bear. A person's body weight or an object's weight is normally 무게, and 하중 comes up when talking about how much a structure can hold. You often see 최대 하중 on safety labels.

examples.en: It is decided by the sum of the two test scores.
Please tell me the result of the total.

examples.ko: 세 달 매출의 합산이 목표를 넘었어요.
examples.en: The combined sales of three months exceeded the goal.
I'm confused about the method of adding up.
I added up wrong, so the total score was off.
I reported the combined amount of all branches.

explain: 합산은 이미 나온 여러 숫자를 한데 모아 더하는 과정에 가까워요. 점수, 매출, 시간처럼 따로 나온 값을 모을 때 써요. 더한 결과 숫자는 '합계'라고 해요.
explain_en: 합산 is closer to the process of gathering several numbers that already exist and adding them. It is used for separate values such as scores, sales, and time. The resulting number is called 합계.

examples.en: I add up the scores of the two subjects.
When I add up all the costs, it comes to 100,000 won.
We totaled the scores and decided the ranking.
When you add up, the units must match.
The total came out higher than I thought.
I was put in charge of adding up the monthly sales.

explain: 합산하다는 '더하다'보다 딱딱해서 보고서, 회의, 뉴스에 어울려요. 장 볼 때 가격을 더하는 일에는 '더하다'나 '계산하다'가 자연스러워요.
explain_en: 합산하다 is stiffer than 더하다, so it fits reports, meetings, and news. For adding up prices while shopping, 더하다 or 계산하다 sounds more natural.

examples.en: That person repented with tears.
I offered a prayer of repentance.
Real repentance is when your actions change.
The theme of that story is sin and repentance.
They say that forgiveness is hard without repentance.
At church there is a time for prayers of repentance.

explain: 회개는 주로 교회와 종교 이야기에서 써요. 일반 대화에서 잘못을 뉘우칠 때는 '반성'이나 '후회'를 써요. 회개는 잘못을 인정하고 삶을 바꾸겠다는 뉘앙스가 있어요.
explain_en: 회개 is used mainly in church and religious talk. In ordinary conversation, when someone feels sorry for a mistake, 반성 or 후회 is used. 회개 carries the nuance of admitting a wrong and promising to change one's life.

examples.en: I deeply repent of my wrongs.
I repented of my sins and started a new life.
If you truly repent, you can be forgiven.

examples.ko: 회개한 사람을 사람들이 다시 받아 줬어요.
examples.en: People accepted the person who had repented again.
I prayed with a repentant heart.
I hoped that you would repent, even if late.

explain: 회개하다는 종교에서 죄를 뉘우치고 마음을 돌이킨다는 뉘앙스가 강해요. 일상에서는 '반성하다'가 훨씬 자연스러워요. 숙제를 안 해서 선생님께 '회개해요'라고 하면 과장되게 들려요.
explain_en: 회개하다 strongly carries the religious nuance of feeling sorry for sin and turning one's heart around. In daily life 반성하다 is far more natural. Telling a teacher '회개해요' for not doing homework would sound exaggerated.

en: script; screenplay (of a play or drama)

examples.ko: 이 드라마의 극본은 유명한 작가가 썼어요.
examples.en: A famous writer wrote the script of this drama.
I practiced while reading the script.
The lines in the script are so funny.
I liked the script, so I decided to appear in it.
I wrote the play script together with a friend.
The actors moved according to the script.

explain: 극본은 연극이나 드라마를 쓴 글이에요. 영화는 '시나리오'라고 하고, 연습하는 현장에서는 '대본'이 더 자주 쓰여요. 드라마 자막에서는 '극본 ○○○'처럼 작가 이름 앞에 써요.
explain_en: 극본 is the written text of a play or a drama. For films, 시나리오 is used, and on set or in rehearsal, 대본 is more common. In drama credits it appears before the writer's name, like '극본 ○○○'.

en: contribute (an article) to a newspaper or magazine

examples.en: The teacher contributed an article to the newspaper.
I contribute a column to a magazine.

examples.ko: 기고할 글을 아직 다 못 썼어요.
examples.en: I haven't finished writing the piece to contribute yet.
The piece I contributed was published today.
I'm preparing a piece to contribute to the school newspaper.

examples.ko: 전문가가 인터뷰 대신 직접 기고하기도 해요.
examples.en: Sometimes an expert writes in directly instead of being interviewed.

explain: 기고하다는 신문, 잡지, 웹사이트에 직원이 아닌 사람이 글을 보낼 때 써요. 그 회사 직원이 쓰는 글에는 '쓰다'나 '취재하다'를 써요. 글은 '기고문', 쓴 사람은 '기고자'라고 해요.
explain_en: 기고하다 is used when someone who is not on staff sends a piece to a newspaper, magazine, or website. For staff writers, 쓰다 or 취재하다 is used. The piece is called 기고문 and the writer is called 기고자.
